The Eight Laws

The Eight Laws

Carved in stone and raised on the village square.
Binding for all folk of the Light freeborn, sworn, merchant, traveler, and child.

:

I. The Law of the Channel

No mortal calls a God with an unbound tongue.
All pleas are carried only through temple rite, shrine oath or consecrated voice.

:

II. The Law of the Seal

No plea without a mark.
Whoever seeks Grace must name self, origin, and bear the Seal of rightful patronage.

:

III. The Law of the Offering

No Grace without an offering.
Before any plea is spoken, payment is given grain, coin, service, blood or vow as need demands.

:

IV. The Law of the Record

Every answered plea must be witnessed.
Miracles and blessings are entered in the House of the Eight: day, place, witnesses and price.

:

V. The Law of Domain

Petition only whom it concerns.
Law to Thyrros, Change to Thronos, Healing to Valkath, Passage to Nethrion,
Freedom to Sylphoria, Trade to Ithkor, Smithing to Xaldris, Fate to Azarath.

:

VI. The Law of the Boundary

No miracle breaks the Order.
None may demand a sign that violently rends harvest, birth, death or the turning of time.

:

VII. The Law of the Mandate

Heresy is theft from the Eight.
Whoever forges seals, steals Grace or defiles rite falls under the Sentinels Mandate.

:

VIII. The Law of the Eighth Day

On the Eighth Day, all is counted, thanked, and cleansed.
Each door renders its due, each household speaks its vow, each quarrel is brought before the shrine.

: Stone-Ending:
Keep these laws and dwell under protection. Break them and call down Judgment.

What the Scriptures of the Eight Teach

The Eight Laws are not presented by the temples as mere restrictions.
In the holy writings of the old faith, they are called the Mercies of Order the sacred form through which divine grace may pass safely into the mortal world.

According to the scriptures, the gods are not absent because they are cruel, but distant because their power is too great to be touched without form, witness, and rightful boundary.
Mortals, the texts claim, were never meant to call heaven with raw desire. Without rite, seal, and offering, prayer becomes hunger and hunger invites ruin.

Thus the faithful are taught that the Laws protect both the soul and the world:

  • the Channel protects prayer from becoming chaos
  • the Seal protects identity from false claim
  • the Offering protects grace from theft
  • the Record protects truth from distortion
  • the Domain protects the world from confusion of power
  • the Boundary protects creation from reckless miracle
  • the Mandate protects the sacred from defilement
  • the Eighth Day protects the people from forgetting their place

In temple teaching, this order is not described as burden, but as mercy.
The scriptures say that the gods gave law because unchecked grace would break the weak, unmake the harvest, disturb the dead, and let prideful mortals seize what belongs only to heaven.

Priests often repeat an old line from the Book of the Eight:

Grace without order becomes fire in dry grain.
Order without grace becomes stone upon the living.
Therefore the Law was given, that mercy may endure.

For this reason, the pious do not see offerings as payment alone, nor records as bureaucracy, nor seals as ownership.
They are taught to see them as signs of right relation:
the mortal kneels, the god answers, the world remains unbroken.

The harshest teaching concerns the Law of the Mandate.
The scriptures declare that false miracles, stolen blessings, forged seals, and unsanctioned rites are not merely crimes, but acts of spiritual theft.
To steal from the Eight is to endanger all people, for it invites corrupted grace, wandering powers, and judgment without measure.

So the old faith taught that the Sentinels were never instruments of cruelty, but guardians against greater catastrophe.
Where they struck, the writings say, they did so to preserve the boundary between mortal need and divine order.

And on every Eighth Day, the same reminder was spoken in shrines, temples, and village squares:

Count what was given.
Cleanse what was stained.
Bind what was vowed.
Return thanks, lest the world forget its order.

To the devoted, the Eight Laws were never chains.
They were the shape of safety.

But to those who suffered beneath them, they were proof that even holy protection may become a cage.

Common Sayings of the Faith
  • “No Grace without witness.”
  • “A seal protects the soul.”
  • “What is unrecorded invites falsehood.”
  • “The Mandate is mercy in iron.”
